summary: Specifies the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol, which carries PPP sessions through an IP network. It is a standards-track protocol.

eli5.summary: A way to wrap one kind of network traffic in another, like a tunnel that carries it across a different network.

questions: what is the difference between lac and lns
how does l2tp set up a tunnel
subtitle: Carry PPP sessions across an IP network by wrapping each frame in a tunnel between an access concentrator and a network server.

tldr.problem: With plain PPP, the dial-up connection and the PPP session must end on the same device, so a user has to dial all the way to the network access server, possibly at long-distance cost.
tldr.mechanism: L2TP lets a nearby L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC) accept the call and tunnel the PPP frames over a packet network, usually UDP port 1701, to an L2TP Network Server (LNS) where the PPP session actually ends. A reliable control channel sets up tunnels and sessions.
tldr.outcome: To the user, there is no functional difference from dialing the network server directly. L2TP can also let multilink PPP channels that arrive at different access servers end at one server. RFC 9601 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 2661 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999 and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 9601, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Tunnel PPP
sections.content:
PPP (RFC 1661) carries multiprotocol packets over layer 2 point-to-point links. Normally a user's layer 2 connection (dialup, ISDN, ADSL and so on) ends at a Network Access Server (NAS), and the PPP session ends on the same device.

L2TP separates the two. The user connects to an access concentrator, such as a modem bank or DSLAM, and the concentrator tunnels individual PPP frames across a packet-switched network to the NAS. The connection can terminate at a local concentrator instead of a distant server, avoiding long-distance toll charges. From the user's perspective, nothing changes.

The same ability helps multilink PPP (RFC 1990), which needs all channels of a bundle to meet at one NAS. With L2TP, calls spread across different physical access servers can all be projected to one NAS. The document defines the control protocol for on-demand tunnel creation and the encapsulation that multiplexes several PPP sessions in one tunnel.
sections.eli5: Normally you must call the faraway office yourself, which is expensive. L2TP lets you call a nearby helper who passes your call along to the office through a shared pipe.

sections.title: LAC, LNS, Tunnels and Sessions
sections.content:
Two roles matter. The L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC) sits between the remote system and the network and tunnels packets to its peer. The L2TP Network Server (LNS) is the logical end of the PPP session being tunneled. A host that runs L2TP natively (a LAC Client) can create a tunnel to the LNS directly, with no separate LAC.

A tunnel exists between a LAC and LNS pair. It consists of one control connection and zero or more sessions, each carrying one PPP stream and mapped one to one with a call. Multiple sessions may share a tunnel, and multiple tunnels may exist between the same pair.

L2TP uses two kinds of message. Control messages set up, maintain and clear tunnels and calls, and travel on a reliable control channel. Data messages carry PPP frames on an unreliable data channel and are not retransmitted when packets are lost. Both ride on an underlying packet transport such as UDP, Frame Relay or ATM.
sections.eli5: The helper near you is the LAC and the office is the LNS. The pipe between them is a tunnel, and each caller gets their own lane inside the pipe, called a session.

sections.title: The L2TP Header
sections.content:
Control and data messages share one header. The T bit says whether the message is data (0) or control (1). The L, S, O and P bits mark optional fields and priority. Optional on data messages, the Length, Ns and Nr fields MUST be present on every control message, so control messages set the L and S bits to 1, and the O and P bits to 0.

Ver MUST be 2. The value 1 is reserved so that older L2F packets can be detected, and packets with an unknown version MUST be discarded. Reserved bits MUST be 0 when sent and ignored when received.

Tunnel ID and Session ID have local significance only: each end assigns its own identifiers, and each message carries the ID chosen by the intended recipient. The value 0 is special and MUST NOT be assigned. It is sent when the peer has not yet assigned an ID, and an Assigned Tunnel ID or Assigned Session ID AVP then identifies the tunnel or session.

Ns counts messages sent and Nr is the number expected next, which together provide reliable delivery on the control channel. The optional Offset Size field tells where the payload starts.
sections.eli5: Every packet wears a label saying whether it is a control note or a conversation, which lane it belongs to, and its number in line so the receiver can tell if something is missing.

sections.title: Control Messages and AVPs
sections.content:
Control message bodies are built from Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs), a uniform encoding meant to maximize extensibility while keeping interoperability. Each AVP has a Mandatory (M) bit, a Hidden (H) bit, a 10 bit length, a Vendor ID, an Attribute Type and a value. The length is 6 plus the value's length, and a single AVP can carry at most 1023 octets. Vendor ID 0 means IETF-defined, while other vendors can use their own Vendor ID for private extensions.

The M bit controls what happens with an unrecognized AVP. If set, the session (or the whole tunnel, if the message concerns the tunnel) MUST be terminated. If clear, the AVP MUST be ignored.

The H bit hides the value, for example a password, which requires a shared secret between LAC and LNS. The value is XORed with an MD5 hash of the attribute number, the shared secret and a random vector sent in a Random Vector AVP that precedes the hidden AVPs.

The control message type is carried in the Message Type AVP: Start-Control-Connection-Request, Reply and Connected (1, 2, 3), Stop-Control-Connection-Notification (4), Hello (6), Outgoing-Call Request, Reply and Connected (7, 8, 9), Incoming-Call Request, Reply and Connected (10, 11, 12), Call-Disconnect-Notify (14), WAN-Error-Notify (15) and Set-Link-Info (16).
sections.eli5: Control notes are made of small labeled slips, like 'name: Sam'. A slip can be marked 'you must understand this one or stop', or sealed so nobody can read it along the way.

sections.title: Setting Up and Tearing Down
sections.content:
First the control connection is built with a three message exchange: SCCRQ, SCCRP and SCCCN, then a Zero-Length Body (ZLB) acknowledgment if nothing else is queued. This step also secures the peer's identity and exchanges version, framing and bearer capabilities. Authentication is optional and CHAP-like: a Challenge AVP in SCCRQ or SCCRP must be answered with a Challenge Response AVP, and a mismatch means the tunnel MUST NOT be established. It uses the same shared secret as AVP hiding.

Then sessions are added, one per call. For an incoming call, the LAC sends ICRQ, the LNS replies ICRP, and the LAC finishes with ICCN. For an outgoing call, the LNS sends OCRQ, the LAC replies OCRP and later sends OCCN when the call is done.

Either side tears down a session with a single CDN message. Either side can close the whole tunnel, and every session in it, with one StopCCN. The receiver acknowledges with a ZLB and keeps enough state to accept retransmissions for a full retransmission cycle, recommended as 31 seconds.
sections.eli5: First the two ends say hello and check each other's secret handshake. After that each phone call gets its own lane. To finish, one side says goodbye, and the other waits a little in case that goodbye got lost.

sections.title: Carrying Frames and Reliable Control
sections.content:
The LAC strips CRC, link framing and transparency bytes from each PPP frame, wraps it in L2TP and forwards it down the right tunnel. The LNS handles it as if it arrived on a local PPP interface. Tunnel and Session IDs let many conversations share one tunnel.

On the data channel, sequence numbers are optional. The LAC can ask for them with a Sequencing Required AVP, and otherwise the LNS turns them on or off by sending data messages with or without them. They detect loss and reordering but do not trigger retransmission. If the tunneled PPP session carries only IP, the LNS might disable them.

Control messages get a sliding-window reliable transport. Ns starts at 0 and wraps modulo 65536. A message is retransmitted if unacknowledged after a recommended default of 1 second, with exponential backoff (a cap, if used, MUST be at least 8 seconds). After several retransmissions, with a recommended default of 5, the tunnel and all its sessions MUST be cleared. An implementation may use a receive window of 1 but MUST accept a window of up to 4. Hello messages serve as a keepalive to tell a dead tunnel from an idle one.

Over IP, L2TP MUST offer UDP encapsulation by default, using registered port 1701. The initiator picks any free source port and sends to port 1701, and ports and addresses must then stay fixed for the tunnel's life. UDP checksums MUST be enabled by default. Because UDP can drop or reorder packets, the RFC warns that loss-sensitive PPP features such as TCP header compression and history-based compression or encryption need care.
sections.eli5: Phone-call data is sent without resending lost bits, since a short glitch is tolerable. The control notes are sent like registered mail: each one is numbered and resent until the other side confirms it arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tunnel authentication has the same security attributes as CHAP. It protects against replay and snooping while the tunnel is set up, but it does not authenticate anything afterwards, and a malicious user who can snoop the tunnel could inject packets once it is established. Assigned Tunnel IDs and Session IDs SHOULD be unpredictable to deter session hijacking.

L2TP itself depends on the transport for confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of its packets. When running over IP, IPsec can protect all L2TP control and data packets, which look like ordinary UDP/IP data to it. This protects tunneled PPP traffic between the LAC and LNS, but it is not a substitute for end-to-end security between hosts.

L2TP also defines AVPs that forward PPP authentication results from the LAC to the LNS. This implies direct trust of the LAC, so an LNS that supports proxy authentication MUST be able to switch it off and require a new round of PPP authentication.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake only checks who you are at the start. To keep outsiders from peeking into the pipe, you need to lock the pipe itself, for example with IPsec.

fields.name: T L x x S x O P x x x x
fields.desc: Type, Length, Sequence, Offset and Priority flag bits; x bits are reserved and set to 0.

fields.name: Length (opt)
fields.desc: Total message length in octets; required on control messages.

fields.name: Tunnel ID
fields.desc: Identifier chosen by the intended recipient.

fields.name: Session ID
fields.desc: Identifier of the session within the tunnel.

fields.name: Offset Size (opt)
fields.desc: Octets past the header where the payload starts, followed by optional padding.
